name: Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE): A Slippery Discovery
era: The Birth of Synthetic Polymers (1907-1938): The Bakelite Revolution
historical_events_referenced: Discovery of nuclear fission (Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, 1938)
The Manhattan Project's Oak Ridge gaseous diffusion plant

historical_images.alt: A French magazine advertisement for Frigéco refrigerators, showing three women in coats and hats admiring an open refrigerator stocked with food, above French advertising copy.
historical_images.caption: The mechanical refrigerator was becoming a mass consumer object across the industrialised world in the 1930s, and its growth is what put a cylinder of experimental refrigerant gas on Plunkett's bench.
historical_images.author: loki11

historical_images.alt: A wooden laboratory bench crowded with 1930s electronic apparatus — vacuum tubes, wired boxes, batteries and glass vessels — displayed behind museum glass, with a diagram of the layout on the wall behind.
historical_images.caption: The apparatus with which Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split the uranium atom in Berlin in 1938, now in the Deutsches Museum. The same year, a DuPont chemist in New Jersey found a molecule that resisted being taken apart by anything at all.
historical_images.author: J Brew

historical_images.alt: A 1963 DuPont magazine advertisement showing a man in a raincoat standing behind a screen of falling rain, with the text 'Even if it rains pea soup' and the Zepel fabric fluoridizer branding below.
historical_images.caption: DuPont spent the 1950s and 60s finding fluorochemistry a life beyond the laboratory bench — Zepel, a fabric treatment built on the same chemistry as Teflon, is one of many trade names PTFE and its relatives wore into the consumer market.
historical_images.author: DuPont Corporation

historical_images.alt: An aerial black-and-white photograph of the enormous U-shaped K-25 gaseous diffusion building at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, surrounded by smaller support buildings and roads.
historical_images.caption: The K-25 gaseous diffusion plant at Oak Ridge, where PTFE gaskets and seals held back uranium hexafluoride gas that would have destroyed almost any other material — a use classified for years after the war.
historical_images.author: James E. Westcott, official US Army Manhattan Project photographer

melt_flow_index.conditions: PTFE has essentially no melt flow even above Tm due to extremely high melt viscosity; processed via sintering, not conventional melt extrusion.

electrical_conductivity.conditions: reciprocal of reported volume resistivity, 1×10¹⁶ Ω·m

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Roy J. Plunkett discovered PTFE accidentally in 1938 at DuPont's New Jersey facility while attempting to synthesize a refrigerant. The 'Teflon' trademark was registered in 1945; commercial production reached over 910,000 kg/year by 1948. Produced via free-radical suspension or emulsion polymerization of tetrafluoroethylene, with persulfate initiators generating the propagating radicals.

structure_morphology.tacticity: Not applicable -- the CF2-CF2 repeat unit has no stereocenter.
structure_morphology.crystal_structure: Polymorphic helical chain packing: Form II below 19 °C (triclinic/pseudohexagonal, a=b≈0.559 nm, c≈1.688 nm, β≈119.3°, 13/6 helix); Form IV 19-30 °C and Form I above 30 °C (trigonal, a=b≈0.566-0.567 nm, c>1.95 nm, 15/7 helix); Form III at high pressure (orthorhombic, 2/1 helix).
structure_morphology.chain_flexibility_notes: The fully fluorinated backbone gives PTFE its extremely low surface energy and low coefficient of friction.
structure_morphology.tg_relation_notes: PTFE has several sub-Tg crystalline transitions in addition to its amorphous glass transition, most notably the ~19-30 °C crystal-disordering transitions (β 292 K, β″ 303 K) that cause a characteristic small volume change near room temperature.

tg.conditions: α (glass I) transition, 399 K; PTFE also shows sub-Tg crystalline transitions (β 292 K, β″ 303 K, γ/glass II 193 K)

tm.conditions: DSC, first (irreversible) melt; reversible/second melt ~327 °C, extended-chain form ~385 °C

decomposition_onset.conditions: decomposition onset; 350 °C reported for 0.001% weight loss

coefficient_of_friction.conditions: static 0.08, dynamic 0.06; against polished steel 0.05-0.08 per Mark 1999

most_chemicals.value: Exceptional resistance; used as a liner for corrosive-material containment

acids.conditions: dilute and concentrated, including fuming nitric acid and aqua regia

limiting_oxygen_index.conditions: >99.5% O2 (effectively non-flammable in air); Mark 1999 reports >95%

solubility_parameter.conditions: 12.7 is the calculated value; an experimental figure of 16.7 is also reported

processing_methods: suspension/emulsion polymerization + cold-press sintering (not melt-processable in the conventional sense)

environmental.environmental_notes: PTFE manufacture has historically been associated with PFOA/PFAS-family processing aids, a significant environmental and regulatory concern for the fluoropolymer industry broadly (specific to PTFE's own persistence: not independently verified).

carcinogenic_classification.value: not listed by ACGIH, NIOSH, NTP

toxicity_safety.safety_notes: Mutagenic, teratogenic, and reproductive toxicity effects not known.
